analysis.investment_thesis: Bajaj Electricals fails both legs of the Magic Formula — earnings yield of ~6.6% (EBIT ₹307 Cr / EV ₹4,648 Cr) is well below the 12% threshold, and ROCE of 11.6% is far below the 20% minimum for a "good" business. At 120x trailing P/E with nine-year revenue CAGR of just 0.6%, the market is pricing in a dramatic turnaround that the fundamentals do not yet support.
key_strengths: Strong operating cash flow — 5/5 years positive OCF (₹347 Cr in FY25), demonstrating basic business viability
Debt dramatically reduced from ₹1,084 Cr (FY20) to ₹243 Cr (FY25), improving balance sheet quality
Promoter holding of 62.7% aligns management with shareholders
key_risks: No revenue growth — 9-year CAGR of just 0.6% (₹4,590 Cr in 2016 vs ₹4,826 Cr in 2025); not a growth business
Net profit in structural decline: ₹216 Cr (FY23) → ₹131 Cr (FY24) → ₹133 Cr (FY25), while the stock trades at 120x earnings
ROCE of 11.6% and ROE of 7.12% signal a low-quality business that earns less than its cost of capital
red_flags: Operating margin reported at -2.10% — the company is destroying value at the operating level in recent reporting
P/E of 120x on stagnant, declining earnings; EV/EBITDA of 33x is extreme for a zero-growth consumer durables firm
Net profit declined ~38% from FY23 peak while stock remains richly valued — clear earnings deterioration
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Running the Magic Formula on Bajaj Electricals produces poor results on both dimensions. Earnings yield (EBIT/EV) = ₹307 Cr / ₹4,648 Cr = 6.6% — barely above the 6% floor where I'd call a stock definitively overvalued, and well short of the 12% that makes a business attractive. Return on Capital (proxied by ROCE) is 11.6%, far below the 20% threshold I require to call a business "good." A company must score well on BOTH metrics; Bajaj Electricals fails both. The combination of a 120x trailing P/E and nine-year revenue CAGR of 0.6% is particularly alarming — the market is essentially pricing in a decade of strong earnings recovery that has not materialized despite multiple years of opportunity.

The balance sheet cleanup (borrowings down from ₹1,084 Cr to ₹215-243 Cr) is commendable, and consistent positive free cash flow (₹318 Cr in FY25) shows the business is not a cash incinerator. However, free cash flow has been declining steadily from ₹871 Cr (FY22) to ₹318 Cr (FY25), driven by lower operating income and rising capex. The Morphy Richards and Bajaj brand portfolio operates in a highly competitive, fragmented consumer durables space with no evident pricing power — operating margins have oscillated between 4-8% for a decade with no upward trend. There is no identifiable moat, no growth, and no margin of safety at current valuations. This is a pass.
